certainty_reasoning: Documented public devotion and close, teasing intimacy: the 1879 poem 'The New Helen', the inscription 'To Helen, formerly of Troy, now of London' in her copy of Poems, Wilde acting as her tutor-amanuensis (her own note calls him 'my kind tutor'), and the warm 'My dear Lil' correspondence continuing after his marriage. Nothing read makes a sexual claim; whether the public devotion was courtship or performance is a real interpretive question, but the documented register is romantic-devotional, so this class fits the read evidence. The 1899 remark about marrying her 'with pleasure' reaches us via Vincent O'Sullivan as printed by the editors - chain noted.
summary: Wilde's public poetic devotion to the great Society beauty of the age - 'The New Helen', the Troy/London inscription - alongside a working intimacy as her tutor and amanuensis and a durable friendship: she is among the first he tells of his engagement, and he sends her theatre stalls in 1885 with news of Constance's confinement.

sources.quote: Of course I'm longing to learn more Latin but we stay here till Wednesday night so I shan't be able to see my kind tutor before Thursday. Do come and see me on that afternoon about six if you can.
sources.context: Lillie Langtry to Wilde, Sunday [c. 1879-80], Beaconsfield, Milehouse, Nr Plymouth - printed in the editors' n. 5, which notes Wilde also acted as her amanuensis and adviser
sources.supports: Langtry's own words for what Wilde was to her - 'my kind tutor' - and the standing invitation to call: the only first-hand statement from her side in the record
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 116 (printed p. 91, folio confirmed), read as page image 2026-08-03.
sources.speaker: Lillie Langtry

sources.quote: Wilde's poem to her, 'The New Helen', appeared in Time for July 1879 and was reprinted, with revisions, in Poems (1881). In Mrs Langtry's copy of this book Wilde wrote: 'To Helen, formerly of Troy, now of London.'
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, main-particulars footnote on Langtry
sources.supports: The public devotion: the poem and the inscription.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 116 (printed p. 91, folio confirmed), read as page image 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: Vincent O'Sullivan records Wilde as saying in 1899: 'The three women I have most admired are Queen Victoria, Sarah Bernhardt, and Lillie Langtry. I would have married any one of them with pleasure.'
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note, quoting O'Sullivan's record of Wilde in 1899
sources.supports: Wilde's own late-life framing of the admiration; reaches us via O'Sullivan as printed by the editors.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 116 (printed p. 91, folio confirmed), read as page image 2026-08-03.

sources.quote: My dear Lil, I am really delighted at your immense success; the most brilliant telegrams have appeared in the papers here on your performance in Peril. … And so, I write half to tell you how glad I am at your triumphs - you, 'Venus Victrix of our age'! - and the other half to tell you that I am going to be married …
sources.context: Wilde to Lillie Langtry, circa 22 January 1884, Royal Victoria Hotel, Sheffield - telling her of his engagement to Constance Lloyd
sources.supports: The durable intimate-friend register ('My dear Lil', 'Venus Victrix of our age'); she is among the first told of the engagement.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF p. 246 (printed p. 224, folio confirmed), read as page image 2026-08-03. Elision drops the American-tour sentences and the description of Constance (that passage is quoted on the constance--wilde record).
